content: In the field of chemistry, an epimer is defined as a type of stereoisomer that differs from another compound in the configuration at only one of its several stereogenic centers. Stereoisomers, in general, include enantiomers and diastereomers, both of which possess at least one stereogenic center. However, geometric isomers, which are a subclass of diastereomers, are excluded from this definition. For instance, the sugars α-glucose and β-glucose are examples of epimers. In α-glucose, the hydroxyl (-OH) group attached to the first (anomeric) carbon is oriented in the opposite direction to the methylene group. Conversely, in β-glucose, the hydroxyl group is aligned in the same direction as the methylene group. These two molecules are not only epimers but also classified as anomers. Another example involves β-D-glucopyranose and β-D-mannopyranose, which are epimers because they differ solely in the stereochemistry at the second carbon position. Specifically, in β-D-glucopyranose, the hydroxyl group at the second carbon is in an equatorial position, meaning it lies in the plane of the ring. In contrast, in β-D-mannopyranose, the hydroxyl group at the second carbon is in an axial position, meaning it projects upward from the plane of the ring. These two molecules are epimers but are not considered anomers. In chemical nomenclature, one member of an epimeric pair is often designated with the prefix epi-. For example, the compounds quinine and epi-quinine are epimers. When the stereoisomeric pairs are enantiomers, the prefix entis used instead.
